The two-chamber geometry is derived from previous RTRC experience with high-pressure conformable composite tanks designed to maximize storage volume while reducing weight and space requirements. Figure 1: Conceptual Phase 2 conformable composite tank 1.2. Subscale Phase 1 Tank Design Figure 2 illustrates the subscale Phase 1 tank planned to be fabricated for thermal testing. The inner hydrogen tank is a cylinder of length 700 mm with 250 mm radius ends and a wall thickness of 3 mm, creating an internal volume of 0.10 cubic meters. There is a 50 mm vacuum gap to the outer shell (to contain multi-layer insulation), with the outer shell wall thickness at 4 mm. Both inner and outer pieces are fiber-wound composite. The outer shell is split at its midline for assembly. Page 3 of 30 Approved for Public Release Figure 2: Phase 1 test tank design 1.2.1. Upper Port and Lower Boss Figure 3 shows the boss design for the hydrogen tank. This boss serves to seal the polar hole at each end of the composite tank, with additional provisions for hydrogen ingress and egress at the upper boss (to be discussed below). A spring-energized C-seals acts against the inner tank to contain the liquid hydrogen. This is a proven seal in a variety of applications, including liquid hydrogen, and consists of a C-shaped jacket of PTFE with a metallic spring element inside. The PTFE jacket seals against the mating surfaces while the inner spring provides a restoring force to the jacket to compensate for PTFE’s reduced elasticity at extreme cryogenic temperatures. Metal components are targeted to be 316 stainless steel, a material that performs well at cryogenic conditions. Figure 3: Boss design with spring-energized seal Page 4 of 30 Approved for Public Release A retaining ring, which is spread and spiraled into the tank during assembly, contacts the inside of the tank and rests against a lip on the inner anchor. The anchor piece threads to the seal bulkhead component to compress the spring-energized seal. A hex cutout in the anchor allows for it to be turned with a wrench while holding the bulkhead to bring the parts together, with a ring of PTFE between the bulkhead and composite tank serving as a spacer to achieve the seal working height. Because the spring- energized seal operates in a controlled gap versus a controlled load, a relatively low load of around 50 lbs. per inch of circumference is transferred to the composite. The seal does require a fine surface finish for optimum performance, so it is planned to use a caul plate during fabrication of the tank in the areas where the seal acts against the composite.
